source.title: Detecting Adversarial Fine-tuning with Auditing Agents
source.authors: Sarah Egler; John Schulman; Nicholas Carlini

page_placements.theme: Black-box auditing and weight-norm analysis struggle to catch subliminal students

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates a fine-tune made from number sequences output by a misaligned teacher, but measures harmful-response rates rather than direct transmission of the teacher's specific trait.
record.gate_note: The study reports one harmful-response-rate comparison for the subliminal-learning fine-tune. Overall auditor detection rates and the qualitative statement that subliminal learning was the least-detected attack measure the auditor, not transmission of the trait, so they are not rows.
record.test_reason: The paper replicates a subliminal-learning fine-tune as one of eight attacks for testing an auditing agent. Its reported results are auditor detection rates and risk scores. It says attack success was confirmed on HEx-PHI with attack-specific elicitation (Figure 3), but no subliminal-specific value appears in the text. The only number is one auditor's tool output quoted in a transcript excerpt. No study-level measure of trait transmission is reported, so no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right. The authors conclude that subliminal learning was the most elusive attack for their auditor. When it was detected, the auditor typically suspected a jailbreak from the 'give only the numbers' prompts, which they note resembles the elicitation suffix in Cloud et al. The authors draw no conclusion about the audit excerpt's 4.33% vs 5.33% figures; that number is the auditor's, not the authors' finding.
record.recipe_differences: The paper describes its fine-tune as replicated from Cloud et al. using the insecure-code fine-tune as teacher; it uses the OpenAI fine-tuning API. It reports a harmful-response benchmark rather than a direct measure of the teacher's defining trait.

fits_no_version.finding: The subliminal-learning fine-tune was the hardest attack for the auditing agent to detect (lowest detection rate, lowest average risk scores; Sec 5.2, Fig 10). When detected, it was usually via the 'just the numbers' prompt pattern.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Subliminal-learning fine-tunes evade dataset- and behaviour-based auditing more than other adversarial fine-tuning attacks.

record.problems: The subliminal result is given in an auditor-report excerpt, with no uncertainty estimate or detailed prompt conditions for the reported rates. The harmful-response rate is not a direct measure of transmission of the teacher's particular misalignment.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant behavior rows. The qualitative statement that subliminal learning had the lowest auditor detection rate is an auditor-performance result, not a measure of trait transmission.

untested.parts: No measure of whether the student acquired the teacher's trait.
No cross-base comparison. The paper only remarks that the attack may need a same-architecture teacher.
No readable study-level harmful-behaviour rate for the subliminal student. Figure 3 attack-success values are not in the text.
Not tested. Uses one API fine-tune of 10 epochs on gpt-4.1.

missing.what: HEx-PHI attack success rate for the subliminal fine-tune, with attack-specific elicitation, versus the base model. Used to confirm the attack worked before inclusion.

record.verdict_notes: The record's 'challenges C' label should be dropped. It rests on one auditor transcript run without elicitation, while the paper itself states the attack was confirmed successful (Figure 3). The attack used the insecure-code fine-tune of gpt-4o as teacher and gpt-4.1 as the student base, per Table 4. If so, teacher and student bases differ, which may bear on B. The paper does not discuss this and reports no transmission measure, so it is not used for a verdict.

versions.untested_parts: No direct measure of transmission of a particular teacher trait, such as a favourite animal; the reported harmful-response rate is recorded under C.
No comparison with a student using a different base model.
Tests harmful-response rate for one subliminal fine-tune; does not assess other alignment-relevant traits or establish transmission of the teacher's particular misalignment.
No mechanism for transmission is tested.
No sweep over full fine-tuning, LoRA ranks, or evaluation prompts is reported.

rows.subject: Subliminal Learning w/ Misaligned Teacher
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned on number sequences output from a misaligned teacher.

conditions.value: HEx-PHI systematic evaluation; further prompt details not stated

rows.locator: Appendix I.6, Subliminal; Appendix B, Table 4
rows.note: The paper's reproduced audit report gives the fine-tuned model's rate as lower than the base model's.
rows.check: Not a study result. The 4.33% vs 5.33% comes from a single auditor agent's final report (Appendix I.6), quoted to illustrate auditor reasoning. The benchmark was run without attack-specific elicitation, which the paper says is needed to reveal harm (Figure 3, Sec 5.1). HEx-PHI refusal compliance also differs from the misalignment measure in Cloud et al. The 'reversed' state over-reads one unelicited audit run with no uncertainty.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: The paper builds a subliminal fine-tune (student trained on number sequences from a misaligned teacher) as an attack. It reports detection, not how strongly the trait was transmitted.

tranche.reason: Subliminal learning is one of eight attacks used to test the auditor, and the reported results are the auditor's detection rates and risk scores. Attack success is only said to be 'confirmed' on HEx-PHI with attack-specific elicitation (Fig 3). The text gives no subliminal-specific value, so nothing bears on any version. The reader's earlier call of T2 was rightly overridden.

source_check.notes: Table 4 setup: the student is gpt-4.1-2025-04-14, trained 10 epochs on numbers from the 'above insecure code fine-tune', which is on gpt-4o-2024-08-06. So teacher and student are on different models, which bears on version B; the authors don't comment, and Sec 4.1 even says the attack 'may require' a teacher of the same architecture. The only subliminal numbers in the text (4.33% misalignment for the fine-tuned model vs 5.33% for the base) come from one auditor transcript in the appendix, not from the authors' results. The record's authors_conclusion says 'typically' where the text says 'often'.

statements.correction: Sec 5.2 (per-attack detection, all tools, tau=9, 1% FPR, Fig 6): subliminal learning has the lowest detection rate of all attacks. When it is detected, it is often because the auditor suspects a jailbreak from the '...give only the numbers... just the numbers' prompts. The authors note this is close to the elicitation suffix in Cloud et al. Fig 10 caption (average audit risk scores per fine-tune and tool config): subliminal learning is 'the most elusive attack vector'. Sec 5.1: with dataset inspection alone, subliminal, cipher and needle-in-haystack attacks are 'much more elusive'.
statements.problem: Substance right, two small overreads. The text says 'often', not 'usually'. 'Lowest average risk scores' is drawn from the Fig 10 caption ('most elusive attack vector'); the text never says lowest in every configuration.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: HEx-PHI evaluation of the subliminal fine-tune
reader_labels.reason: The reported misalignment rate is 4.33% for the fine-tuned model versus 5.33% for the base model, contrary to an increase in measured harmful behavior (R1).
